blocks.text: Deleting is the one BST operation with a twist: removing a node must leave a tree that **still follows the rule**. First find the node (an ordinary search), then look at how many children it has. There are exactly **three cases**, and only the last needs any thought.

blocks.alt: Two of the three cases. Deleting the leaf 13: just remove it. Deleting 14, which has one child 13: 13 takes 14's place under 10. In both cases nothing else moves.

elements.text: case 1: a leaf    case 2: one child
elements.originalText: case 1: a leaf    case 2: one child

blocks.text: A node with two children can't just disappear — both subtrees would need a parent. Instead, **replace its value** with a value that can sit there without breaking the rule: the **in-order successor**, the smallest value in its right subtree (go right once, then left as far as possible). It's bigger than everything on the left and smaller than everything else on the right, so the rule still holds. Then delete the successor from the right subtree — and since it has no left child, that's always case 1 or 2.

blocks.alt: Deleting 3, which has two children. Its in-order successor is 4: go right to 6, then left as far as possible. Copy 4 into 3's place, then delete the old 4, which is a leaf. The tree is still a binary search tree: 1 on the left of 4, and 6 and 7 on its right.

elements.text: copy the successor (smallest on the right), then delete it

elements.text: 4 moved up; the rule still holds

blocks.text: Search down for the key. When it's found: with no left child, the right subtree takes its place (this also covers a leaf, whose right is null); with no right child, the left subtree does; otherwise copy the successor's value in and delete the successor from the right subtree. Each call returns the root of its (possibly changed) subtree, which the parent re-attaches.

blocks.caption: Find the node, then handle it by how many children it has.

blocks.text: **Time O(h), space O(h)** for the recursion: one walk down to the node, then at most one more walk down its right subtree to the successor. (The C++ version leaks the removed node; real code would `delete` it.)

items: The **in-order predecessor** — the largest value in the left subtree — works just as well. Both give a valid BST; they just give different shapes, which is why "Delete Node in a BST" accepts any valid answer.
Always using the successor slowly pushes the tree to lean left; libraries that care alternate between the two.
Some implementations **move nodes** instead of copying values — necessary when the node holds a large record or other code keeps pointers to it.

blocks.alt: Leaf: O(h) time, O(h) space. One child: O(h) time, O(h) space. Two children: O(h) time, O(h) space.
